> Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.
> “Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest that cadets will be trained in racial profiling and planting evidence.
> Given that blistering analysis of American law enforcement, you might imagine that actual cops aren’t big fans of the latest GTA title, which was released after a 13-year wait on Thursday. Yet as millions of gamers have started to explore every stash house and back alley in the sun-drenched wilderness of a fictionalized South Florida, even police departments have attempted to exploit this monocultural mania to elevate their public messaging or recruit new officers.
> It’s a curious strategy given that the series rewards theft and drug dealing while enticing you to run over pedestrians, but evidently the mere presence of law enforcement in the games (as the primary antagonists, mind you) was enough to inspire waves of AI slop celebrating the thin blue line.
> An Instagram channel of the San Diego Police Department, for example, on Thursday posted an AI-generated image of an SDPD cruiser set against a sunset over the San Diego Bay. Its neon pinks and purples match the saturated aesthetic of GTA, and in case there was any doubt what the department was going for, the nonsensical phrase “Join San Diego PD VI” appears at the top. “Want to drive a police car, we can make that happen!” reads the caption. “Apply Now!”
> Another police department in Washington state shared GTA-like imagery on its Instagram page, encouraging viewers to try “the real-life version” of GTA VI by pursuing a career in law enforcement. “No cheat codes,” the caption advertised. “No respawns. Just real people, real challenges, and a career that makes a difference.” A wave of self-serious GTA slop also flooded the feeds of police departments in Canada, from Edmonton to Toronto—though the Calgary Police Service tried something more lighthearted by having one of their traffic officers react to clips of dangerous and illegal driving maneuvers in the game.

Having acquired assets including Grubhub and Blue Apron, the company operates a vertically integrated model featuring automated food preparation and a diverse multi-brand delivery platform, with AI-driven menu development and an estimated valuation of $9 billion.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.
> Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.
> Founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.
> Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the company announced it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.
> Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The company has outlined ambitious growth plans, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.
> Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit company Blue Apron, restaurant delivery platform Grubhub, media company Tastemade, and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.
> Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create, its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop new food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.
> Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.
> Despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.

The company reports a $7 billion ARR with its cloud data warehouse contributing $1.5 billion at 100% year-over-year growth, alongside rapid monetization of its Lakebase agentic platform.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> There’s a funny kind of game that the latest of late-stage startups must play when raising money. They often have to sell more shares than they want or risk offending some of their existing VCs.
> This scenario recently played out with AI big-data company Databricks and its latest $5 billion raise announced Thursday, co-founder and CEO Ali Ghodsi (pictured above) told TechCrunch.
> “We wanted to raise $1 billion, but then The Information printed this article saying that Databricks is doing a big fundraise. They did that in the middle of our conference. We were heads down with our conference, and we were not actually at all focused on fundraising,” Ghodsi recalled, referring to a conference that took place in June.
> “As soon as that article went out, there was a long line of investors that started calling. My phone blew up. It was like the worst timing for us because we were busy with our conference,” he said.
> It was an enviable problem that turned the news report into a self-fulfilling prophecy.
> “The interest level was just insane. Just from this select group of investors that we looked at, there was $15 billion of interest,” he said.
> When there’s that much desire to get into a deal, telling some long-term backers no is a recipe for hard feelings. Databricks decided to issue more stock, and in July, sent out a press release announcing it had closed its new round at a $188 billion valuation. (The company didn’t disclose at the time how much it had raised.)
> On Thursday, Databricks shared it raised $5 billion from a paragraph worth of VCs that it let in on the deal and that its valuation pushed higher to a nice round $190 billion. The $5 billion round was led by Coatue and several others, including Blackstone, MGX, various accounts associated with various arms of T. Rowe Price, and new investor Sixth Street Growth. (Sixth Street is the firm founded by former Goldman Sachs chief investment officer Alan Waxman.) About two dozen VCs were named as participants.
> Why were they all so eager? Databricks seems like a sure bet.
> Ghodsi said his company has hit $7 billion of annualized run rate revenue, which is currently growing at 80% and is cash-flow positive. Its core product, a cloud data warehouse, is $1.5 billion of that run rate, and still growing at 100% year-over-year, he said.
> Plus, Databricks has the magic AI pixie dust. Its database for agents, Lakebase, launched in June, 2025, and has hit $100 million revenue run rate. Its AI chatbot tool Genie, that can do business analysis on the spot, “is insanely popular,” he said.
> So, if the business is doing so well, why raise more capital? The company had already raised $20 billion over the past 20 months.

- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/6c09f2fbfa88888c

- Executive Summary: SpaceX's AI coding platform, Cursor, informed the U.S. House Committee on Homeland Security and the Select Committee on China that it is exploring the phase-out of the Kimi K2.5 model from Chinese lab Moonshot AI due to geopolitical risks. Investigations revealed that several U.S. firms adopted Chinese models for cost and performance advantages, prompting lawmakers to propose a national American open-weight AI initiative to reduce reliance on foreign models.

* [Regulatory & Investigation Focus] Cursor aims to phase out Chinese Moonshot AI models following regulatory scrutiny.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Legislators propose a national initiative for open-weight models to ensure technical sovereignty.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk,"CNBC has learned.
> Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.
> It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington. The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.
> But now Cursor plans to "explore phasing out PRC [People's Republic of China]-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk,"according to a report produced by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared exclusively with CNBC ahead of its publication on Friday.
> The report, which follows a months-long investigation into the adoption of Chinese AI models into the American tech stack, said Cursor "informed the Committees"of those plans. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the investigation about their use of Chinese AI models.
> SpaceX announced it entered into a formal agreement to buy Cursor in June; the deal was completed in August. SpaceX is developing the Grok family of models, which Cursor has been involved in training.
> Cursor, SpaceX and DoorDash did not respond to a CNBC request for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
> ### Chinese AI adoption
> The report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance of Chinese AI models were driving adoption, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at "price and performance the market demands."
> "Beijing is now seeking to turn those technological gains into global market share and long-term dependence,"the report says. China's embassy in the U.K. did not respond to a request for comment. China's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond.
> It also sets out recommendations to address the issues it has identified.
> Those include launching a "national American open-weight initiative"that combines public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and "lawful access"to American frontier models for training.
> The report also says an order, made public in October, that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, should be built on, by prohibiting the use of "PRC-developed AI models"in federal information systems and in performance of federal contracts.

### Artificial Analysis says Inkling 2 Mini, with 5.4B active parameters, matches Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) on its Intelligence Index with ~5x fewer active parameters (Artificial Analysis)
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/eed97af23850c34f
- Primary Source: Artificial Analysis (https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/inkling-2-mini)
- Executive Summary: Thinking Machines has released the open-weights Inkling 2 Mini model, utilizing a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 26B total and 5.4B active parameters. By employing looped Transformer layers, the model achieves performance parity with Qwen3.8 27B while utilizing only 20% of the active parameters, all under an Apache 2.0 license.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Thinking Machines: Released Inkling 2 Mini with high efficiency MoE architecture
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To improve Pareto frontier efficiency between model intelligence and compute cost
* [Key Metrics] Features 26B total/5.4B active MoE looped architecture with 1M context window.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Efficiency: achieves parity with Qwen3.8 27B using ~5x fewer active parameters and ~2.8x less compute.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an open weights looped transformer on the Pareto frontier for Intelligence vs. Active Parameters
> Inkling 2 Mini is a 26B total, 5.4B active parameter mixture-of-experts model. The 5.4B active parameter count includes three passes through its looped layers; it uses 3.1B unique weights per text token, and it is small enough to run on a MacBook or DGX Spark.
> It is released under an Apache 2.0 license, with text and image input and a 1M token context window.
> Inkling 2 Mini matches Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) and Nanbeige4.3-33B on the Intelligence Index with ~5x and ~6x fewer active parameters, respectively.
> It is on the Pareto frontier for Intelligence vs. size on both total and active parameters.
> Inkling 2 Mini uses ~38% more output tokens than Qwen3.8 27B for the same Intelligence Index score, but ~2.8x less compute.
> Twelve of its 24 layers run three times per token, adding compute without adding output tokens. It averages ~152K output tokens per Intelligence Index task vs. ~110K for Qwen3.8 27B and ~158K for Nanbeige4.3-33B. On our compute proxy measure (active parameters × tokens), it sits on the Pareto frontier, using ~2.8x less compute than Qwen3.8 27B and ~5x less than Nanbeige4.3-33B.
> Inkling 2 Mini is ~6x cheaper and ~4x faster per task than Qwen3.8 27B.
> It costs $0.59 and takes 9.0 minutes per Intelligence Index task vs. $3.53 and 38.2 minutes for Qwen3.8 27B. GPT-6 Luna (max) scores 28 for $0.15 per task. Cost uses Thinking Machines' first-party pricing ($0.15/$0.50/$0.015 per 1M input/output/cache hit tokens).
> OpenAI’s release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol delivers the #2 model in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and most of the Cost per Task Pareto frontier

This prompted widespread backlash and shop closures from creators, despite claims from James Ossman, VP of customer operations, that data use is restricted to fraud detection and advertising, as users remain concerned about the lack of opt-out mechanisms and potential IP exploitation.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Many longtime owners of shops on Etsy, the online marketplace known for its handmade goods, said this week that they had left the site over a policy change that they said leaves them vulnerable to exploitation by artificial intelligence companies.
> Language in Etsy’s new terms, set to take effect on Dec. 16, says the company and its “third party partners and vendors” reserve the right to use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”
> The terms say that Etsy and its partners will use such technologies in part to improve the platform and keep it safe for users. The previous version of the terms did not include a clause about using content for artificial intelligence.
> “Etsy decided that selling on their platform now means letting them train AI on our artwork AND resell that data to third parties, with no way to opt out,” Aaron Millard, an illustrator, wrote in an Instagram post announcing that he was deleting the shop that he has run for nearly a decade. “My work took years to learn and create. I won’t let it be stolen.”
> Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus, the founders of the home goods and stationary brand Cognitive Surplus, which has sold its products on Etsy for 13 years, also deleted their shop. In an Instagram post, they accused the company of claiming “perpetual, free, boundless permission to not only train AI on our art, but also to resell the data for profit.”
> “For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus said in an interview. “We don’t want anything to do with that.”
> In a statement posted to Etsy’s website on Monday, James Ossman, the company’s vice president for customer operations, addressed the site’s sellers directly.
> Etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote. He cited the development of fraud detection tools and advertisements on the site as among the reasons for granting third parties access to sellers’ content.
> A representative for Etsy did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
> Many publicly traded internet companies like Etsy have been caught between pressure from shareholders to embrace artificial intelligence and the ire of users who reject the technology.
> Big bets by major firms and their investors on the A.I. revolution have helped the U.S. stock market set records in recent years. But Americans in general are much less enthusiastic. A Gallup poll from the summer found that nearly 40 percent of Americans feel that A.I. does more harm than good. - Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Canadian retail spending is expected to have declined in October, following a 0.8% increase in September led by gasoline stations and fuel vendors.
> A preliminary estimate points to a 1.5% decrease in retail sales last month, which would be the largest decline since February 2025.
> Sales in September increased in five out of nine subsectors, and rose by 6.9% at gasoline stations and fuel vendors. That increase was largely driven by higher prices, as sales in volume terms increased by a more modest 1.6%.
> Economists surveyed by Bloomberg had expected retail sales increased by 0.7% in September.
> Core retail sales, which exclude gasoline stations and fuel vendors as well as motor vehicle and parts dealers, increased by 0.1%. In volume terms, sales were also up by 0.1%.
> The largest decline in core retail sales was food and beverage retailers, which was led by a 0.5% decline at grocery stores, following a 1% increase in August.
> Building material and garden equipment and supplies dealers declined by 1.3%, while furniture, home furnishings electronics and appliances retailers decreased by the same magnitude.
> Meanwhile, retail sales increased by 1.2% in the third quarter. In volume terms, they rose by 1% over the three-month period.
> The expected decline in October retail sales provides further evidence of weakening to start the fourth quarter, said CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham.
> “While the 1.5% decline estimated for October will partly reflect lower gasoline prices, most of that move lower in pump prices has actually occurred in November rather than October, and as a result this advance estimate suggests a decline in volumes as well,” Grantham said in a note to investors.
> The Canadian economy — including consumer spending — has remained largely resilient throughout the U.S. trade war. However, growth is expected to slow in the second half of the year after the dispute escalated and more tariffs were imposed by both countries.
> The labour market has also shown signs of weakness, as employment has failed to grow this year. Servus Credit Union chief economist Charles St-Arnaud said the stagnant labour market in recent months may be to blame for weaker retail sales.
> “This is another indicator that suggests that the Canadian economy is losing momentum going into the last few months of 2026. The weakness suggests the Bank of Canada should take a pause to better assess the situation before hike again, especially with some fuel prices easing in recent weeks,” St-Arnaud said in an email.
> Despite the expected slowdown, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to clamp down on inflationary pressures from higher energy prices. Traders in overnight swaps put the odds of a hike in December at about 60%, which would further weigh on spending.

### TML releases Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights 26.4B-parameter transformer that loops middle layers three times per token for better reasoning with fewer tokens (Thinking Machines Lab)
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/d95c866cf08800ae
- Primary Source: Thinking Machines Lab (https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/)
- Executive Summary: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights model with 26.4B parameters, utilizing a 'looped transformer' architecture that executes middle layers three times per token. This design enhances reasoning capabilities for agentic coding and serial tasks while maintaining a 20GB memory footprint suitable for local deployment on consumer hardware.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Thinking Machines Lab (AI Open Source Community): Released Inkling 2 Mini with 26.4B parameters, looped architecture, and local deployment optimization
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To balance reasoning depth with computational efficiency
* [Key Metrics] 20GB memory footprint for a 26.4B parameter model.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Optimized for local deployment and on-device customization.
- Strategic AI Analysis: {'briefing_zh': 'Thinking Machines LabInkling 2 Mini26.4B“”token20GB', 'briefing_en': "Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights model with 26.4B parameters, utilizing a 'looped transformer' architecture that executes middle layers three times per token. This design enhances reasoning capabilities for agentic coding and serial tasks while maintaining a 20GB memory footprint suitable for local deployment on consumer hardware.", 'elements_zh': {'who': '', 'where': 'AI', 'what': 'Inkling 2 Mini26.4B', 'why': ''}, 'elements_en': {'who': 'Thinking Machines Lab', 'where': 'AI Open Source Community', 'what': 'Released Inkling 2 Mini with 26.4B parameters, looped architecture, and local deployment optimization', 'why': 'To balance reasoning depth with computational efficiency'}, 'insight_zh': 'agentic AI', 'insight_en': 'The shift from sheer parameter scaling to looped weight execution marks a critical pivot in optimizing logic efficiency for edge-side high-intensity inference. By reusing depth rather than stacking weights, this architecture lowers memory costs and improves chain-of-thought transparency, offering a more accessible paradigm for commercial agentic AI deployment.', 'digest_zh': 'Thinking Machines LabInkling 2 Mini26.4B“”token20GB', 'digest_en': "Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights model with 26.4B parameters, utilizing a 'looped transformer' architecture that executes middle layers three times per token. By reusing depth rather than stacking weights, this architecture lowers memory costs and improves chain-of-thought transparency, offering a more accessible paradigm for commercial agentic AI deployment.'}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.
> Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.
> Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).
> We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.
> We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.
> Most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.
> Open video: PlaneBench flight simulator demo, screen with phone video inset0:0015× Loading the flight simulator Inkling 2 Mini built… To try the flight simulator, open this page on desktop. Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.
> Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.
> Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind on...

### Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/ce34ecfa0fba02bc
- Primary Source: Ars Technica (https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/a-leaky-ai-supply-chain-is-exposing-secret-user-data-at-an-alarming-rate/)
- Executive Summary: HD Moore, Chief Research Officer at Dragos, uncovered major security flaws in the AI supply chain by injecting 2 million trackable 'canary' secrets into AI prompts sent via routing services. The investigation found evidence of prompt theft, disregard for zero-data-retention (ZDR) settings, and unauthorized logging of user prompts by intermediaries, posing significant compliance risks.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] HD Moore (CRO of Dragos): Injected 2 million trackable 'canaries' into prompts to audit security, uncovering widespread data leaks and privacy violations
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To verify the security and compliance of sensitive data handling within the complex AI supply chain
* [Key Fact Detail] Supply chain audit using 2 million canary credentials.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Widespread failure of Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policy enforcement.
- Strategic AI Analysis: {'briefing_zh': 'DragosHD MooreAI200“Canaries”AIAI', 'briefing_en': "HD Moore, Chief Research Officer at Dragos, uncovered major security flaws in the AI supply chain by injecting 2 million trackable 'canary' secrets into AI prompts sent via routing services. The investigation found evidence of prompt theft, disregard for zero-data-retention (ZDR) settings, and unauthorized logging of user prompts by intermediaries, posing significant compliance risks.", 'elements_zh': {'who': 'HD MooreDragos', 'where': 'AI', 'what': '200', 'why': 'AI'}, 'elements_en': {'who': 'HD Moore (CRO of Dragos)', 'where': 'AI routing and intermediary service platforms', 'what': "Injected 2 million trackable 'canaries' into prompts to audit security, uncovering widespread data leaks and privacy violations", 'why': 'To verify the security and compliance of sensitive data handling within the complex AI supply chain'}, 'insight_zh': 'AI“”', 'insight_en': 'The fragmented ecosystem where AI apps connect through intermediaries to multiple suppliers has become a black-box liability for corporate compliance. The current supply chain lacks end-to-end trust, and the failure of ZDR enforcement and unauthorized logging suggest that existing regulatory frameworks and commercial pledges are highly fragile against complex multi-hop call chains.', 'digest_zh': 'DragosHD MooreAI200“Canaries”AIAI', 'digest_en': 'DragosHD MooreAI200“Canaries”AIAI', 'key_points_zh': ['200', 'AI', 'ZDR'], 'key_points_en': ['Supply chain audit using 2 million canary credentials', 'Exposure of unauthorized prompt logging and credential theft via AI routers', 'Widespread failure of Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policy enforcement'], 'takeaway_zh': 'AI“”', 'takeaway_en': 'The fragmented ecosystem where AI apps connect through intermediaries to multiple suppliers has become a black-box liability for corporate compliance. The current supply chain lacks end-to-end trust, and the failure of ZDR enforcement and unauthorized logging suggest that existing regulatory frameworks and commercial pledges are highly fragile against complex multi-hop call chains.'}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.
> The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.
> ### Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations
> To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of AWS access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.
> The findings are striking. They included:
> Evidence that at least three AI providers were compromised by attackers who used their access to siphon prompts they received
> Multiple resellers in the inference marketplace that logged the prompts and somehow passed them along to people who used the credentials
> Multiple cases of AI providers not following end-user privacy settings embedded into flags specifying terms such as Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or “no data collection”
> “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”
> Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool...

### OpenAI makes it much harder for attackers to extract how its latest AI models think
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/e34d6438927ff1c3
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/openai-makes-it-much-harder-for-attackers-to-extract-how-its-latest-ai-models-think/)
- Executive Summary: OpenAI has deployed layered security mechanisms for GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol models, reducing the success rate of black-box inference-extraction attacks from 54% to under 0.2% through targeted training, input/output filtering, and API access restrictions. These measures are designed to neutralize distillation attacks that attempt to reconstruct core reasoning paths, supplemented by the weekly suspension of tens of thousands of illicit accounts.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> OpenAI has sharply tightened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal automated tests, attacks pulling protected reasoning from prior requests dropped from a 54.0 percent success rate on GPT-6 Astra to 0.2 percent on GPT-6.2 Astra. Attacks on active requests fell from 22.9 to 0.9 percent, OpenAI says. The company is now bringing selected improvements to GPT-6 Astra, too.
> The defenses work on two levels. For individual requests, the systems combine targeted training, input and output filters for messages and tool calls, and API blocks that stop older models from reading protected reasoning. Against coordinated campaigns, OpenAI bans thousands to tens of thousands of accounts weekly.
> Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red teaming against GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower is better.
> Anthropic is fighting systematic distillation attacks as well, also banning tens of thousands of accounts to curb the theft of internal reasoning, reportedly succeeding in 90 to 99 percent of cases. Anthropic has also called for a coordinated response from industry and policymakers.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone and Telefónica are in early talks to form a consortium that would bid for European satellite spectrum and offer calls, texts and data to ordinary phones from orbit, Bloomberg reported on Monday. The service would compete with Starlink on its home continent.
> Paula Doenecke, Gian Volpicelli and Clara Hernanz Lizarraga cited people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified. No decision has been taken on the consortium or on whether it will bid, they said. All four operators declined to comment to Bloomberg. TNW has not independently verified the report.
> The prize is a slice of the 2 GHz band that Brussels wants to reserve for a European-controlled operator. The four companies together serve most of the mobile customers in the EU’s largest markets. If they bid as one, the reserved third of the band has an obvious winner before the auction opens.
> The band in question is the 2 GHz mobile satellite services spectrum, a 30 MHz pairing that lets a handset keep a connection where no mast reaches. The current licences, held by Viasat and EchoStar since 2009, expire in May 2027. The European Commission proposed on 27 May to run a single EU-level selection for the next licences and to split the band in three.
> One third would go to a company under majority European control. One third would go to sovereign government services, delivered through IRIS², the EU’s own constellation. The final third would be open to anyone, including SpaceX and Amazon. TNW reported the shape of the plan the day before the Commission adopted it.
> The proposal still has to pass the European Parliament and the Council. The carriers are organising for an auction whose rules do not yet exist in law.
> Direct-to-device is the one satellite service that reaches a mass market without new hardware, and Starlink dominates it. SpaceX can already send texts, data and calls to unmodified phones from orbit, and it sells that capability through mobile operators, including Deutsche Telekom, Bloomberg noted. What it cannot do in the EU is offer the service on its own, because it does not hold the spectrum.
> That is the leverage the consortium would be bidding for. An operator that holds the European third of the band decides whether Starlink is a supplier or a competitor in its market. Four operators holding it together decide that for most of the continent.
> The awkward part is that two of the four already have American partners. Deutsche Telekom has an agreement with SpaceX to offer Starlink’s direct-to-device service. Vodafone owns half of a joint venture with AST SpaceMobile, the Texas company building its own phone-to-satellite network. Under the Commission’s proposal, that 50/50 structure would not qualify as European-controlled, and Vodafone wou...

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.
> While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.
> But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.
> According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED.
> After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.”
> “It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said.
> In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified.
> Board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia.

- Executive Summary: Signal has implemented screenshot blocking on iOS 27 and specific Android versions to counter OS-level AI agents like Siri, Gemini, and Meta's Muse, which can scrape screen contents. Signal warns that these AI agents, often leveraging system-level permissions or accessibility tools, undermine end-to-end encryption by extracting decrypted messages directly from the display interface.

* [Core Event] Signal (Communication Platform) (iOS 27 and Android OS): Blocking screenshots to prevent AI agents from scraping chat data via accessibility tools

* [Key Technical Spec] Signal blocks system-level screenshots to prevent AI scraping.
* [Official Stance & Demand] Calls for standardized OS-level controls to restrict AI access to specific applications.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Signal is restricting screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats. The app blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protection on supported Android versions when an AI assistant tries to access the screen. Signal warned Reuters of an "existential threat"to privacy.
> OS-level AI like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture screen content to complete user tasks. That undermines end-to-end encryption by letting agents pull decrypted messages straight from the display and process them externally.
> Meta's AI agent Muse recently captured Signal content on Android and macOS through broad setup permissions, including accessibility tools and screenshots on macOS. Meta says this happened only with explicit user permission.
> Signal already blocked Microsoft's Recall on Windows but calls its defenses incomplete: macOS screenshots can't be reliably blocked, and AI access to file systems and notifications remains a risk. Signal says Apple, Google, and Microsoft should make it easy to block AI agents from apps entirely.

### Canada Retail Sales Tracking Largest Decline Since Feb. 2025
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/a849dc2414d03369

- Executive Summary: Statistics Canada reports an estimated 1.5% decline in retail sales for October, marking the sharpest drop since February 2025. CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham noted that the decline reflects broader volume contraction and stagnant labor market growth, signaling weakening economic momentum heading into the final quarter of 2026.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Statistics Canada, CIBC Senior Economist Andrew Grantham: Retail sales estimated to decline by 1.5%, the largest drop since Feb 2025
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Weakening consumer demand, fuel price volatility, and stagnant labor market
* [Key Metrics] 10% retail sales expected to fall 1.5%, significantly below forecasts.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Analysts suggest the Bank of Canada pause tightening to monitor economic resilience.

Internal demand weakness, exacerbated by external trade frictions, suggests a shift toward a prolonged period of low-growth economic cycles.', 'digest_zh': '9101.5%CIBC·Andrew Grantham', 'digest_en': 'Statistics Canada reports an estimated 1.5% decline in retail sales for October, marking the sharpest drop since February 2025. Internal demand weakness, exacerbated by external trade frictions, suggests a shift toward a prolonged period of low-growth economic cycles.'}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Canadian retail spending is expected to have declined in October, following a 0.8% increase in September led by gasoline stations and fuel vendors.
> A preliminary estimate points to a 1.5% decrease in retail sales last month, which would be the largest decline since February 2025.
> Sales in September increased in five out of nine subsectors, and rose by 6.9% at gasoline stations and fuel vendors. That increase was largely driven by higher prices, as sales in volume terms increased by a more modest 1.6%.
> Economists surveyed by Bloomberg had expected retail sales increased by 0.7% in September.
> Core retail sales, which exclude gasoline stations and fuel vendors as well as motor vehicle and parts dealers, increased by 0.1%. In volume terms, sales were also up by 0.1%.
> The largest decline in core retail sales was food and beverage retailers, which was led by a 0.5% decline at grocery stores, following a 1% increase in August.
> Building material and garden equipment and supplies dealers declined by 1.3%, while furniture, home furnishings electronics and appliances retailers decreased by the same magnitude.
> Meanwhile, retail sales increased by 1.2% in the third quarter. In volume terms, they rose by 1% over the three-month period.
> The expected decline in October retail sales provides further evidence of weakening to start the fourth quarter, said CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham.
> “While the 1.5% decline estimated for October will partly reflect lower gasoline prices, most of that move lower in pump prices has actually occurred in November rather than October, and as a result this advance estimate suggests a decline in volumes as well,” Grantham said in a note to investors.
> The Canadian economy — including consumer spending — has remained largely resilient throughout the U.S. trade war. However, growth is expected to slow in the second half of the year after the dispute escalated and more tariffs were imposed by both countries.
> The labour market has also shown signs of weakness, as employment has failed to grow this year. Servus Credit Union chief economist Charles St-Arnaud said the stagnant labour market in recent months may be to blame for weaker retail sales.
> “This is another indicator that suggests that the Canadian economy is losing momentum going into the last few months of 2026. The weakness suggests the Bank of Canada should take a pause to better assess the situation before hike again, especially with some fuel prices easing in recent weeks,” St-Arnaud said in an email.
> Despite the expected slowdown, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to clamp down on inflationary pressures from higher energy prices. Traders in overnight swaps put the odds of a hike in December at about 60%, which would further weigh on spending.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Google now lets Gemini handle Mac tasks in the background. The new "Computer Use"feature in the Gemini Mac app completes multistep tasks across local files, desktop apps, and websites. Google says users simply describe a goal, and Gemini clicks, types, and navigates menus and forms. Everything runs in an isolated background window with a live chat preview, keeping the screen and cursor free for uninterrupted work.
> Users choose which apps Gemini can access, watch every step live, pause anytime, and approve key actions beforehand. Google's examples include batch-editing photos and 3D scenes, filling out shipping forms from local PDFs, and building presentations.
> Computer Use rolls out in English in the US today, and the Gemini Mac app is available to download. OpenAI has also focused on Computer Use recently, pulling well ahead with its Astra model.

It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”

> Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> YouTube has reached an agreement in principle to pay around $3B to thousands of US school districts that accuse it of harming students’ mental health, Bloomberg reported. The deal includes new safeguards for teens and needs most districts to sign on.
> YouTube is finalising a settlement of around $3B with thousands of US school districts, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The districts accuse it of building an addictive platform that harmed students’ mental health.
> It would be the largest corporate settlement ever reached with US school districts. The agreement in principle also includes new safeguards for teens. Google declined to comment, as did the lawyers leading the districts’ cases.
> The deal needs a majority of the districts to sign on and will likely take a few months to finalise. The districts want money back for the costs of social media addiction, such as extra counselling for students. Schools are a key market for Google, which also faces pushback from its own staff over AI in student Search.
> More than 10,000 lawsuits have been filed against YouTube, Meta, Snap and TikTok over the past five years. They claim features such as endless scrolling and autoplay have caused addiction, anxiety and depression in young people. Earlier this year, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube liable in the first bellwether trial.
> Meta agreed in August to settle with nearly every US state for about $18B, by its own count, and to cap teens’ scrolling at two hours a day. In May, YouTube paid just over $2M to a Kentucky school district that also sued Meta, Snap and TikTok. In June, it settled with a teenager to avoid a second California trial.
> The next school case, brought by a district in Tucson, Arizona, is due to go to trial in February. Meta, TikTok and Snap remain defendants.

### The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/0682a15d33147059
- Primary Source: MIT Tech Review (https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/20/1149399/the-most-misunderstood-graph-in-ai-just-got-a-major-update/)
- Executive Summary: Nonprofit evaluation group METR has updated its time-horizon plot for AI capabilities, indicating that models show exponential growth in verifiable tasks like coding and mathematics, but lag in judgment-based tasks that lack automated verification. The report highlights the technological bottleneck in applying reinforcement learning to complex, open-ended research decisions, a capability critical for future autonomous R&D.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Nonprofit evaluation group METR has updated its time-horizon plot for AI capabilities, indicating that models show exponential growth in verifiable tasks like coding and mathematics, but lag in judgment-based tasks that lack automated verification.
* [Context & Motivation] The report highlights the technological bottleneck in applying reinforcement learning to complex, open-ended research decisions, a capability critical for future autonomous R&D..
* [Key Fact] A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
- Strategic AI Analysis: {'briefing_zh': 'METRAIAIAI', 'briefing_en': 'Nonprofit evaluation group METR has updated its time-horizon plot for AI capabilities, indicating that models show exponential growth in verifiable tasks like coding and mathematics, but lag in judgment-based tasks that lack automated verification. The report highlights the technological bottleneck in applying reinforcement learning to complex, open-ended research decisions, a capability critical for future autonomous R&D.', 'insight_zh': '', 'takeaway_zh': ''}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
> The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , due to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.
> The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than the tasks in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt the task many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.
> It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential to AI systems automating research and development.
> And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month weeks ago, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI capabilities progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.
> METR researchers have worked to incorporate some of these fuzzier, judgment-laden tasks that could be most relevant to AI research and ...

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
> Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.
> The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
> A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
> The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
> Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
> In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
> OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
> OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal r...
